name: Security Incident Reporting — Process, Report Structure & Communications
command: # No CLI command — procedural framework reference for writing security incident reports
description: End-to-end framework for security incident reporting. Covers incident identification (security tooling, human observation, third-party notification), categorization (Malware/Phishing/DDoS/Unauthorized Access/Data Leakage/Physical Breach), severity (P1-P4), the 7-step reporting process, proper incident report structure (Executive Summary → Technical Analysis → Impact Analysis → Response/Recovery → Diagrams → Appendices), internal/external communications strategy, channel security requirements (encryption, MFA, ephemeral/air-gapped), and regulatory dimensions (GDPR, breach notification timelines, chain of custody). Real-world example: SampleCorp INC2019-0422-022 — malicious PDF (Adobe Reader vuln) + buffer overflow on HR01 port 31337 → Metasploit C2 at 192.168.220.66:4444, detected via double-encoded PowerShell + VirusTotal (metacoder/shikata).
notes:
=== INCIDENT IDENTIFICATION ===
Sources that trigger incident reporting:
  Security Systems/Tooling   → SIEM alerts, EDR detections, IDS/IPS triggers, AV hits
  Human Observations         → employees noticing anomalies, helpdesk reports
  Third-Party Notifications  → external researchers, partners, law enforcement, CERT

Common incident types:
  Malware            → ransomware, trojan, worm, spyware
  Phishing           → email-based social engineering (malicious attachments/links)
  DDoS               → volumetric/application layer flood attacks
  Unauthorized Access → credential compromise, privilege escalation, insider threat
  Data Leakage       → exfiltration of sensitive/PII/proprietary data
  Physical Breach    → unauthorized physical access to systems/premises

=== INCIDENT SEVERITY ===
P1 — Critical   → Severe impact, ongoing, requires immediate escalation (full breach, ransomware)
P2 — High       → Significant impact, time-sensitive (confirmed compromise, data access)
P3 — Medium     → Moderate impact, not immediately critical (phishing attempt, policy violation)
P4 — Low        → Minimal impact, informational (failed auth, minor anomaly)

=== THE 7-STEP REPORTING PROCESS ===
1. Initial Detection & Acknowledgement
   → Detect via security tooling OR human observation
   → Acknowledge and formally open the incident

2. Preliminary Analysis
   → Scope the incident — determine affected systems and potential impact
   → Apply severity (P1-P4) and incident type classification

3. Incident Logging
   → Log every action, observation, and finding
   → Preferred platforms: JIRA, TheHive Project
   → Fallback: spreadsheet, pen and paper
   → NEVER stop logging; everything is evidence

4. Notification of Relevant Parties
   Internal:
     → IT, Legal, PR, Executive team
     → Organization-wide if impact is severe enough
   External:
     → Customers, partners, regulatory bodies, general public (if warranted)

5. Detailed Investigation & Reporting
   → Full forensic/technical investigation (can span days to years)
   → Comprehensive artifact collection and analysis

6. Final Report Creation
   → Finalized incident report for regulators, insurers, and executive leadership
   → Documents the incident, its origins, timeline, and remedial actions

7. Feedback Loop
   → Post-incident review to identify gaps and improve future preparedness

=== INCIDENT REPORT STRUCTURE ===

--- Executive Summary (non-technical audience) ---
Incident ID          → Unique identifier (e.g., INC2019-0422-022)
Incident Overview    → Type, date/time, duration, affected systems/data, status
Key Findings         → Root cause, CVEs exploited, data compromised/exfiltrated
Immediate Actions    → Isolation, root cause identification, third-party engagement
Stakeholder Impact   → Customer downtime, financial impact, employee/partner risk

--- Technical Analysis (detailed, evidence-based) ---
Affected Systems & Data:
  → All systems accessed or definitively compromised
  → Volume of data exfiltrated (if measurable)

Evidence Sources & Analysis:
  → Tools and methodology used (SIEM queries, traffic analysis, memory forensics)
  → Screenshots and log excerpts as supporting evidence
  → Hash files for evidence integrity (SHA-256)

Indicators of Compromise (IoCs):
  → C2 IPs/domains, malicious file hashes, unusual processes, scheduled tasks
  → Enable hunting across broader environment and threat attribution

Root Cause Analysis:
  → Underlying cause (unpatched software, misconfiguration, weak credentials)
  → Exploited CVEs if applicable

Technical Timeline:
  Phases to document:
    - Reconnaissance
    - Initial Compromise
    - C2 Communications
    - Enumeration
    - Lateral Movement
    - Data Access & Exfiltration
    - Malware Deployment/Activity (process injection, persistence)
    - Containment Times
    - Eradication Times
    - Recovery Times

Nature of the Attack:
  → TTPs used (MITRE ATT&CK framework recommended)
  → Specific tools and frameworks identified (Metasploit, Cobalt Strike, etc.)

--- Impact Analysis ---
  → Quantify and qualify damage to data, operations, and reputation
  → Financial loss, regulatory penalties, reputational damage assessment

--- Response and Recovery Analysis ---
Immediate Response:
  Revocation of Access:
    → How compromised accounts/systems were identified
    → Exact timeframe of detection and revocation
    → Methods: disable accounts, change permissions, firewall rules
  Containment Strategy:
    → Short-term: isolate affected systems (VLAN segmentation, network isolation)
    → Long-term: network segmentation, zero-trust implementation

Eradication:
  Malware Removal:
    → Identification method (EDR, forensic analysis, VirusTotal)
    → Removal techniques (specialized tools, manual removal)
    → Verification (checksum, heuristic analysis for remnants)
  System Patching:
    → CVE(s) addressed, patch management process, fallback procedures

Recovery:
  Data Restoration:
    → Backup validation (checksum verification before restore)
    → Restoration process (step-by-step, including decryption if needed)
    → Data integrity checks (SHA-256 hashing post-restore)
  System Validation:
    → Security hardening before bringing systems back online
    → Operational load/stress tests before production return

Post-Incident:
  Monitoring: enhanced behavioral analytics, new SIEM correlation rules
  Lessons Learned: gap analysis, recommendations, future strategy

--- Diagrams ---
  Incident Flowchart        → Attack progression from initial entry to propagation
  Affected Systems Map      → Network topology with color-coded compromised nodes
  Attack Vector Diagram     → Attacker navigation through defenses (arrows/nodes)

--- Appendices ---
  Log Files, Network Diagrams (pre/post), Forensic Evidence (disk images, memory dumps),
  Code snippets, IR Checklist, Communication Records, Legal/Regulatory Documents,
  Glossary and Acronyms

--- Best Practices ---
  → Root Cause Analysis: always find root cause to prevent recurrence
  → Community Sharing: share non-sensitive details with defender community
  → Regular Updates: keep all stakeholders updated throughout IR process
  → External Review: consider third-party validation of findings

=== COMMUNICATIONS ===

--- Internal ---
Immediate Notification  → alert all relevant internal stakeholders at acknowledgement
Regular Updates         → consistent briefings on status, ramifications, pending actions
Feedback Loop           → channel for teams to share findings, concerns, suggestions

--- External ---
Affected Parties        → direct communication with customers, clients, partners
Public Statement        → for significant incidents; avoid technical jargon
Regulatory Bodies       → notify ICO (UK), DPA (EU) within mandated timeframes
                          GDPR Art. 33: 72-hour notification to supervisory authority
                          GDPR Art. 34: notification to data subjects if high risk

--- Communication Channel Security ---
Encryption              → end-to-end encryption for all incident-related communications
Authentication/AuthZ    → MFA required; restrict access to authorized personnel only
Data Integrity          → cryptographic hashing to ensure messages unaltered in transit
Ephemeral Comms         → auto-destructing messages for top-secret discussions
Air-Gapped              → isolated systems if primary comms backbone is compromised

--- Regulatory Dimensions ---
Data Privacy Laws       → GDPR compliance when discussing/sharing EU personal data
Breach Notification     → jurisdictional timelines; content must meet legal requirements
Record-Keeping          → balance ephemeral messaging vs. regulatory retention requirements
Cross-Border Comms      → data sovereignty laws when incident spans national borders
Chain of Custody        → maintain unbroken documentation if legal action is anticipated

=== REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE — SampleCorp INC2019-0422-022 ===

Incident ID: INC2019-0422-022 | Severity: P2 (High) | Status: Resolved

Attack Chain:
  00:27:27  Employee on WKST01 opens cv.pdf in Adobe Reader 10.0 (outdated/vulnerable)
            → Malicious payload executes via Acrobat Reader vulnerability
  00:35:09  Unauthorized entity (192.168.220.66) accesses dirs with source code + API keys
  00:50:18  Reconnaissance discovers buffer overflow in proprietary HR app (port 31337)
            → Exploit crafted; shellcode establishes reverse shell to 192.168.220.66:4444
  01:30:12  Unencrypted DB on HR01 accessed (SSNs, salary); compressed + exfiltrated via SSH
  02:30:11  SOC/DFIR detect unauthorized activity → VLAN segmentation isolates WKST01, HR01
  03:10:14  Host security solution deployed to affected systems for additional data collection
  03:43:34  Firewall rules updated to block C2 IP 192.168.220.66
  04:11:00  Malware removed from both systems with specialized removal tool
  04:30:00  Adobe Reader updated to patched version on all systems
  05:01:08  Compromised API keys revoked
  05:05:08  User credentials reset (cv.pdf user + recent logins to WKST01/HR01)
  05:21:20  WKST01 restored from verified backup
  05:58:50  HR01 restored from verified backup
  06:33:44  Emergency patch deployed for buffer overflow vuln in proprietary HR app

Affected Systems:
  WKST01.samplecorp.com (192.168.220.200) → dev environment, source code, API keys
  HR01.samplecorp.com   (192.168.220.101) → HR system, employee PII, payroll, SSNs

IoCs:
  C2 IP:   192.168.220.66
  C2 Port: 4444 (reverse shell from HR01 buffer overflow)
  Malicious file: cv.pdf
  cv.pdf SHA256: ef59d7038cfd565fd65bae12588810d5361df938244ebad33b71882dcf683011

TTP Detection (Metasploit):
  Double-encoded PowerShell command observed:
    powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -c $c=new-object net.webclient;...;IEX
  SOC decoded → identified Metasploit PowerShell reflection payload (open source intel)
  Shellcode extracted from PCAP → exported as a.bin → submitted to VirusTotal
    Result: 12/58 vendors flagged; labels: metacoder, shikata (Metasploit signatures)

Root Cause:
  1. Insufficient network access controls (unauthorized device connected via Ethernet)
  2. Outdated Acrobat Reader with known vulnerability
  3. Buffer overflow in proprietary HR application (port 31337)
  4. Inadequate network segregation of critical systems
  5. No user awareness training for phishing/malicious documents

Remediation:
  → Patched Adobe Reader; emergency-patched HR app buffer overflow
  → Implemented network access controls + VLAN segmentation
  → Revoked API keys, reset credentials, blocked C2 IP
  → Adopted behavioral analytics in Elastic SIEM
  → Initiated security awareness training program
  → Forward strategy: zero-trust model, improved email filtering

examples.label: Incident severity classification — P1 (Critical)
examples.command:
# P1=Critical: active ransomware, full domain compromise, critical infrastructure down
# P2=High: confirmed breach, unauthorized data access (SampleCorp example)
# P3=Medium: phishing attempt, policy violation, isolated anomaly
# P4=Low: failed auth attempt, minor/informational anomaly

examples.label: IoC documentation format for incident report
examples.command:
# IoCs to document:
# C2 IP:  192.168.220.66
# C2 Port: 4444
# File hash: ef59d7038cfd565fd65bae12588810d5361df938244ebad33b71882dcf683011 (cv.pdf SHA256)
# User-Agent: Windows-Update/7.6.7600.256 (example from shell.exe)
# Registry persistence: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

examples.label: Verify file integrity with SHA-256 (evidence preservation)
examples.command:
# Windows PowerShell:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 cv.pdf

# Linux:
sha256sum cv.pdf

examples.label: VirusTotal shellcode submission (extract from PCAP first)
examples.command:
# Wireshark: File → Export Packet Bytes → save as a.bin
# Submit a.bin to VirusTotal for AV signature matching
# Metasploit indicators: 'metacoder', 'shikata' in vendor labels

examples.label: Scdbg — analyze shellcode behavior without executing
examples.command:
# Identify shellcode callback and port from buffer overflow payload:
scdbg.exe /f bof2.bin
# Output shows: connect to 192.168.220.66:4444 (reverse shell target)

examples.label: GDPR breach notification timeline
examples.command:
# Art. 33: notify supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware
# Art. 34: notify affected data subjects without undue delay if high risk
# ICO (UK) / relevant national DPA must be notified
# Document: nature of breach, categories/volume of data, likely consequences, measures taken
